extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers of science evaluating empirical laws and apparent exceptions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, classifying, and resolving apparent exceptions to scientific laws — including verification of facts, distinguishing types of exceptions (singular, divergent, accidental, limiting), and using experiment and analysis to reconcile them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish universal vs general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: General should mean that which is true of a whole genus or class; universal principles admit no single exception while general principles may be more frequently obeyed than violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every true statement must be true of some assigned or assignable class. If exceptions exist they must be mentioned (e.g., 'All liquids, except water below 4°C, expand by heat'). Avoid using 'generally true' to mean merely 'true in the majority of cases.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify whether a supposed exception is really a fact
rubrics_metrics.description: When a supposed exception to a law of nature is brought to notice, the first inquiry ought properly to be — Is there any breach of the law at all? It may be that the supposed exceptional fact is not a fact at all, but a mere figment of the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the origin of the claim, consider mental conditions or mistaken observation (example: King Charles' fish-in-bucket weight anecdote). Do not accept assertions without verification; trace causes of false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test asserted facts by careful experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent exceptions should be tested with appropriate trials rather than only refuted by theoretical counter-arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use suitable precautions and accurate observation (example: dropping a stone from a mast or tower to test Copernican objections). Detect small effects with precise measurement (Benzenberg's small eastward deflection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for misapprehension or misidentification
rubrics_metrics.description: Many apparent breaches arise from a misapprehension of the case (e.g., mistaking composite crystals for single crystals or confusing substances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closer observation, microscopy, continuity inference, and chemical analysis to detect composite specimens or differences in hydration (examples: crystals with apparent re-entrant angles due to two crystals; arseniate vs phosphate differing in water of crystallisation; vanadium oxide misidentified as metallic vanadium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek congruent deeper explanations rather than assuming law failure
rubrics_metrics.description: A law may present results that appear in conflict with it because its action is complicated, disguised, reversed, or operating under additional conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explanations that reconcile the phenomenon with the law (examples: buoyancy explained by relative gravity; total internal reflection explained by undulatory theory; missing comet due to perturbing bodies). Apparent breaches often yield to extended analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and expect singular exceptions (special parameter cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular exceptions are single or unique cases which, while obeying the general law, stand out as apparently different (analogous to singular mathematical solutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When laws are expressed mathematically expect singular points (examples: the Pole Star's apparent immobility; couples in mechanics producing rotation instead of a resultant; optical phenomena like rotation of plane of polarisation and conical refraction). Treat these as opportunities for deeper verification and mathematical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat divergent exceptions as extremes of probability or accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Divergent exceptions are phenomena of unusual magnitude or frequency (extreme deviations) that do not imply new laws but arise from probability or accumulated effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply probability theory to judge whether observed frequencies exceed expectation (examples: runs of all-heads in coin tosses, exceptional human heights, extreme storms, rare simultaneous eclipses). Regard unusual conjunctions as possibly expected extreme events unless shown to be more frequent than probabilistic theory predicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute accidental exceptions to extraneous interfering causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidental exceptions arise from casual interference of extraneous causes; the law is in operation but other causes supervene producing apparent failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for interfering conditions such as chemical replacement, films, contamination, or physical barriers (examples: pseudomorphic crystals formed by later deposition, mercury adhesion in barometer tubes, non-conducting vapour films causing spheroidal ebullition, oxide films passivating iron in acid). The presence of such causes explains apparent anomalies without discarding the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider limiting exceptions where laws are inapplicable beyond bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Some phenomena may appear to breach a law because the law is inapplicable beyond certain limits (a limiting exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the domain of applicability of the law (example discussion: total internal reflection might be seen as a limiting case but is explained by wave theory showing no breach of the general law). Explicitly state limits when formulating laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical analysis and extended theory to reconcile apparent anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrepancies between theory and observation often yield to more complete mathematical analysis or extension of theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ refined mathematical methods and consider additional forces or interactions (examples: Clairaut resolving motion of lunar apsides; Léverrier's perturbation studies; mathematical treatment of coupled circular motions explaining optical rotation).
